explanations.explanation: That's the complaint, friend. They said, “It is futile to serve God. What have we gained by keeping His requirements…” It's like working overtime all month and then staring at your paycheck with your lip poked out. The LORD heard every word of it.

Time never comes up, friend. Their complaint was about what they gained: “What have we gained by keeping His requirements and walking mournfully before the LORD of Hosts?” Nobody in this verse checks a calendar. They check what they got out of it and say it's nothing.

Priests aren't in this part at all, friend. The people say “we,” as in “What have we gained by keeping His requirements…” They're talking about themselves. Their words were that serving God is futile, and nobody here passes the job to anybody else.
True, and it's a rough one. In verse 15 they say, “So now we call the arrogant blessed.” They went and said it out loud. Then they said evildoers prosper and even test God and escape.

It's actually true, friend. The text says the people said, “So now we call the arrogant blessed.” That's the LORD quoting their words back to them. They asked what they had spoken against Him, and this is part of the answer.

explanations.answer: Those who feared the LORD and honored His name
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The scroll was written “…regarding those who feared the LORD and honored His name.” They spoke with one another, the LORD listened and heard, and then the scroll was written before Him. Somebody got a whole record made, friend. Not even my cookie box gets that kind of paperwork.

explanations.answer: Those who said serving God was useless
explanations.explanation: Close to the neighborhood, but no, friend. Verses 14 and 15 are where the words about serving God being futile show up. The scroll is about “…those who feared the LORD and honored His name.” That's who spoke with one another and got heard.

explanations.answer: Those who served as priests in the temple
explanations.explanation: No priests in this verse, friend. The text says the scroll was about “…those who feared the LORD and honored His name.” That's all it says about who they are. It names a heart toward the LORD, not a job title.

explanations.answer: Spare them like a man spares his son
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. The LORD says, “…I will spare them as a man spares his own son who serves him.” A son who serves his father, friend. That's the picture He picked. I'd say that's about as close as a picture gets.

explanations.answer: Pay them like a man pays his workers
explanations.explanation: Pay is a good guess, friend, but the text doesn't use it. The LORD says He will spare them “…as a man spares his own son who serves him.” It's a son in this picture, not a paycheck. I don't see a pay stub anywhere in this verse.

explanations.answer: Move them to a new land of their own
explanations.explanation: No moving trucks here, friend. The verse never mentions a new land. The LORD says He will spare them “…as a man spares his own son who serves him.” What He says is sparing, and the picture is a father and his son.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, “So you will again distinguish between the righteous and the wicked, between those who serve God and those who do not.” Those two pairs sit side by side. After all that talk about the arrogant being called blessed, He says you'll see the difference again.

Foolish sounds like it could fit, friend, but it isn't in the verse. The LORD says “…the righteous and the wicked…” Those words line up with “…those who serve God and those who do not.” The word foolish never shows up.

I see why you went there, friend. The people did say evildoers prosper in verse 15. But the LORD's line is about “…the righteous and the wicked…” not rich and poor. He's talking about who serves God and who doesn't, and a bank balance doesn't tell you that.

That's who. The LORD says “…all the arrogant and every evildoer will be stubble…” I think this one is heavy, friend, so I'll just read it plainly. He also says “Not a root or branch will be left to them.”

explanations.answer: Those who fear the LORD's name
explanations.explanation: It's the other way around, friend. The stubble is “…all the arrogant and every evildoer…” Then in verse 2 the LORD turns to “…you who fear My name…” and it's a very different picture for them.
Kings and armies aren't named here, friend. The LORD says “…all the arrogant and every evildoer will be stubble…” That's the group the verse points to. No other group gets added to the list.

That's it. The LORD says, “…the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings…” It's for those who fear His name. I love that the picture here is healing, friend. A sunrise after all that stubble talk.

A pillar of fire does show up in Scripture. It lit the night for Israel as the LORD went ahead of them (Exodus 13:21). But in this verse, the LORD says “…the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings…” Different picture, friend.

A cloud went ahead of Israel by day, along with the pillar of fire by night (Exodus 13:21). That's a different moment, friend. This verse says “…the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings…” It rises, and it brings healing.

Leap! The LORD says, “…you will go out and leap like calves from the stall.” Picture the door swinging open and everybody bouncing out. I can hop and dive face-first into the chocolate chips, gold base and all, but these folks do it way better.
Hiding is the opposite of this picture, friend. The verse says they will “…go out and leap like calves from the stall.” They go out, and they leap. Nobody is ducking behind the door.

Rest is a nice thought, friend, but the verse has more bounce than that. The LORD says, “…you will go out and leap like calves from the stall.” Calves leaping out of the stall are not calves taking a nap. I'd take that over my afternoon slump any day.

explanations.answer: The law of His servant Moses
explanations.explanation: That's right. The LORD says, “Remember the law of My servant Moses, the statutes and ordinances I commanded him for all Israel at Horeb.” Moses was Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10). The word is remember, friend, and it's for all Israel.

explanations.answer: The songs of His servant David
explanations.explanation: David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), is a fine servant to think of, friend. But he isn't in these verses. The LORD says, “Remember the law of My servant Moses…” It's the statutes and ordinances He commanded Moses for all Israel.

explanations.answer: The dreams of His servant Joseph
explanations.explanation: Joseph, one of Jacob's sons (Genesis 35:24), isn't named here, friend. The LORD is the one speaking, and He says, “Remember the law of My servant Moses, the statutes and ordinances I commanded him for all Israel at Horeb.” No dreams in this verse, just the law.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD.” He sends him before the Day comes. That's a prophet showing up ahead of the main event.

Samuel was a prophet (1 Samuel 3:20), friend, but he isn't the name in this verse. The LORD says, “…I will send you Elijah the prophet…” That's the one He sends before the great and awesome Day of the LORD.

Isaiah was a prophet too (2 Kings 19:2), friend, but the name here is different. The LORD says, “…I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD.” It's good to know your prophets, though. Plenty of names on that list.
Yes, fathers goes in the first blank. The LORD says Elijah “…will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children…” That's a heart turning toward the children, friend.
Yes, children goes in the second blank. The verse says, “…and the hearts of the children to their fathers.” So it goes both directions, friend. Hearts turning toward each other.

Priests aren't in this verse, friend. The text says Elijah “…will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers.” It's about fathers and children, and the turning goes both ways.

No kings in this one, friend. The verse is about fathers and children: “…the hearts of the fathers to their children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers.” It's a family picture, and a heart-turning one.

Prophets aren't the hearts being turned here, friend. The verse says Elijah “…will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers.” They turn toward each other, one way and then the other.
